title: Not this, not this
hook: the Upanishad describes the ultimate only by saying what it is not

segments.voice: Yesterday, the universal form: Arjuna saw everything at once and asked for the familiar face back. Your line was overwhelmed. What felt too big yesterday? Today, another Indian text tries the opposite move. Instead of showing everything, it takes everything away. Day one thousand ten.

Try describing a silence. You can't say what it sounds like, because it doesn't sound like anything. All you can do is list what's missing. No traffic. No voices. No engine idling down the street. You describe it by taking things away, and when you've taken enough away, the other person knows exactly what you mean. One of the Upanishads, the Brihadaranyaka, tries this with the biggest subject of all. It reaches for the ultimate reality, and its answer is two words, said twice.
screen: `DESCRIBE A SILENCE.` → `LIST WHAT'S MISSING.` → `TWO WORDS, SAID TWICE.`

segments.voice: First, the pictures. Before it gets to the two words, the passage pictures the form of the person within, in a run of vivid images: something like a saffron-colored cloth, like white wool, like a flame, like a white lotus, like a sudden flash of lightning. Bright, beautiful, quick. Each one catches a glimpse. Second, the turn. Then the text stops and says, in effect: now the teaching. Not this, not this. In Sanskrit, neti neti, a phrase read as two small words run together, na and iti: not thus. All those images were pointing. None of them is the thing. Third, why that isn't a shrug. You might hear not this, not this as giving up. The text hears it the other way. It says there is nothing higher than this not-this. The refusal is the teaching. Whatever you can picture, point at or put in a sentence is smaller than what the passage is after, so the honest description is to keep saying no to every description. Fourth, where it leads. The same passage gives a name for what can't be named: the truth of truth. And some Hindu schools, especially Advaita Vedanta, use neti neti as a practice of the mind. Set aside the body: not this. Set aside the thoughts: not this. Set aside the feelings: not this. What remains when you've said no to everything you can observe, they say, is the one doing the observing. The method is subtraction, all the way down.
screen: `SAFFRON CLOTH, LIGHTNING, A LOTUS.` · `NOW THE TEACHING: NOT THIS.` · `NOTHING HIGHER THAN THIS NOT-THIS.` · `THE TRUTH OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `NETI NETI.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit with what can't be named. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. When a sound arrives, notice it, and say inwardly: not this. When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, a memory, notice it: not this. When a feeling arrives in the body, an itch, a warmth: not this. You're not pushing anything away. You're just declining to call it the whole story. Between the not-thises, rest in whatever is left. If you pray, the quiet can be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Neti neti. Sanskrit for not this, not this: the Upanishad's way of pointing at the ultimate by saying no to every description of it. Today's word.
Your line: the refusal is the teaching. Today, when a label for yourself shows up, my job, my mood, my mistake, try one quiet not this, and see what's left. Day one thousand ten.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, teachers use neti neti as a method of inquiry, setting aside the body, thoughts and feelings as 'not this' to point toward the self that observes them.

original.note: Sanskrit: not this, not this (na iti, not thus), Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.3.6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a way of saying nobody knows.
what it means: every picture points at the ultimate, and none of them is it, so the teaching keeps saying no.
what a scholar hears: na iti, not thus, after a run of images, with the claim that nothing is higher than this not-this, and the name the truth of truth.

not arrayed like one of these

notes: Paraphrased throughout. Max Müller's Upanishads (SBE 15, 1884) is public domain but not on the validator's list and exact wording not certain to this writer. Confirm the list of images in 2.3.6 (saffron-colored cloth, white wool, indragopa insect [omitted], flame, white lotus, sudden flash of lightning) and the lines 'now the teaching: not this, not this, for there is nothing higher than this not-this' and 'the truth of truth' (satyasya satyam).
Etymology neti = na + iti ('not thus') is standard; confirm.

The Advaita Vedanta practice of negating body, thoughts and feelings is described as what 'some Hindu schools' do; 'especially Advaita Vedanta' is a judgment, confirm or trim. Other Vedanta schools read neti neti differently; not named.
Hook names the Brihadaranyaka as 'one of the Upanishads': fine.
Editor: replaced the fridge in the hook (a fridge already appeared on days 1003 and 1008), softened the na iti gloss to 'read as', and cut the superlative 'the most honest'.

Audit (2026-10-01): the images in 2.3.6 describe the form of the person (purusha), not the ultimate itself; teach and fork now say so. Replaced the strawman myth (neti neti means always, always) with one the teach supports (the truth of truth).
